content: The World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends the use of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine for all pregnant women living in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission in Africa. However, resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine among malaria parasites has been steadily increasing in certain regions. Additionally, pregnant women infected with HIV who are on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis cannot use sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine due to the risk of harmful drug interactions. This situation underscores the urgent need to identify alternative medications for malaria prevention during pregnancy. One potential alternative is mefloquine. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of mefloquine for preventing malaria in pregnant women. The study also aimed to assess how factors such as HIV status, gravidity (number of pregnancies), and the use of insecticide-treated nets might influence the effects of mefloquine. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and others, up to January 31, 2018. They also reviewed references, contacted study authors, and sought unpublished data and raw trial results. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing mefloquine IPT or prophylaxis with placebo, no treatment, or alternative drug regimens. Two independent reviewers screened the identified studies, applied inclusion criteria, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. When necessary, they contacted trial authors for additional information. The analysis used risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes, incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for count outcomes, and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes, all presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach for key outcomes, including maternal peripheral parasitaemia at delivery, clinical malaria episodes during pregnancy, placental malaria, maternal anemia at delivery, low birth weight, spontaneous abortions, stillbirths, dizziness, and vomiting. The analysis included six trials conducted between 1987 and 2013 in Thailand, Benin, Gabon, Tanzania, Mozambique, and Kenya, involving a total of 8,192 pregnant women. These trials included women of all ages and gravidities, with gestational ages at recruitment ranging from 16 to 28 weeks or later. Two trials were double-blinded, and only one trial had a low risk of detection bias for safety outcomes. When compared to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, IPTp with mefloquine reduced maternal peripheral parasitaemia at delivery by 35% (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.86; high-certainty evidence). However, it had little or no effect on placental malaria infections (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.86; low-certainty evidence). Mefloquine showed little or no difference in the incidence of clinical malaria episodes during pregnancy (IRR 0.83, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.05; high-certainty evidence). It reduced maternal anemia at delivery (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.94; moderate-certainty evidence) but had little or no effect on the proportion of low birth weight infants (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.17; high-certainty evidence) or on rates of stillbirths and spontaneous abortions (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.58; moderate-certainty evidence). However, mefloquine was associated with significantly higher rates of drug-related vomiting (RR 4.76, 95% CI 4.13 to 5.49; high-certainty evidence) and dizziness (RR 4.21, 95% CI 3.36 to 5.27; moderate-certainty evidence). When compared to cotrimoxazole in HIV-infected women, IPTp with mefloquine plus cotrimoxazole reduced maternal peripheral parasitaemia at delivery by 48% (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.93; moderate-certainty evidence) and reduced placental malaria by 72% (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.57; moderate-certainty evidence). However, it had little or no effect on the incidence of clinical malaria episodes during pregnancy (IRR 0.76, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.76; high-certainty evidence), maternal anemia at delivery (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.20; moderate-certainty evidence), low birth weight rates (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.60; moderate-certainty evidence), or rates of spontaneous abortion and stillbirth (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.42 to 2.98; very low-certainty evidence). Mefloquine was again associated with higher risks of drug-related vomiting (RR 7.95, 95% CI 4.79 to 13.18; high-certainty evidence) and dizziness (RR 3.94, 95% CI 2.85 to 5.46; high-certainty evidence). In conclusion, mefloquine demonstrated greater efficacy than sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in HIV-uninfected women and greater efficacy than cotrimoxazole in HIV-infected pregnant women for preventing malaria infection. It was also associated with a lower risk of maternal anemia and did not adversely affect pregnancy outcomes such as stillbirths, spontaneous abortions, low birth weight, or prematurity. However, the high frequency of mefloquine-related adverse events, particularly vomiting and dizziness, presents a significant challenge to its use as a preventive treatment for malaria in pregnant women.
